notes:
I worked through verses 25–49 using David Guzik (Enduring Word) and the older commentaries collected on BibleHub, StudyLight and Blue Letter Bible: Constable, Keil & Delitzsch, Gill, Matthew Henry, Ellicott, Pulpit, Barnes, JFB, Poole, Clarke, Coke, Coffman and Cambridge. I ran out of search and fetch allowance before I could read the Catholic/Orthodox sites, the NET Bible notes or Bible Odyssey, so there is nothing from those below. Verses I couldn't find anything on are left out.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Introduction (vv. 22–35):** Four messages announce God's judgment on Jerusalem for her unfaithfulness (Ezekiel 23:22-35). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 25:**
- Constable says cutting off the nose and ears was a punishment for adulteresses in the ancient Near East. It fit because such women wore nose-rings and earrings, and it was also used on prisoners of war. Its effect would be to make Jerusalem repulsive to other nations. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Benson explains "jealousy" as God acting against Judah as a jealous man is against his wife. The Chaldeans would carry out His wrath. Benson also reports that Jerome said the Chaldeans often mutilated adulterers this way. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-25.htm
- Coffman adds that God handed Judah over to be judged by her enemies' laws rather than His own. He notes this punishment was not allowed under God's law, but in Mesopotamia it was the frequent punishment of unfaithful wives. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-25.html
- **A difference in how to read it.** Keil says the phrase is not about the Egyptian penalty for adultery. Instead it stands for the mutilation of prisoners captured by their enemies. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-25.htm
- Some read the nose and ears as symbols. Gill reports Jewish interpreters (Jarchi, Kimchi) who took the "nose" as the king and the "ears" as the priest. Henry mentions the same view, and the Geneva notes read it as destroying princes and priests. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-25.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_023.cfm
- Hengstenberg (in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary) takes the nose and ears as the nation's military strength. The two "remnants" are the fighting men, who fall by the sword, and the city's houses, which burn. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-27.html
- Henry takes the remnant falling by the sword as those who had escaped famine and plague. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-25.html

**v. 26:** Constable says stripping her clothes and jewelry may mean losing her wealth, possessions and temple treasures. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 27:**
- Constable: God would let this happen to teach Jerusalem to loathe Egypt as a political partner. — same URL
- Guzik's summary: the judgment had a cleansing purpose. It would purge gross idolatry from the Jewish people so thoroughly that it would never return in the old form. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-23/

**vv. 28–29:**
- Constable identifies "those you hate" as the Babylonians, who would rob Jerusalem and leave her naked in 586 B.C. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Coke says the sisters could expect no pity from those they had rebelled against. in the greatness of their punishment the greatness of their crimes will appear. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Henry on "exposed" (v. 29): when a criminal is punished, his old sins are dragged into the open. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-25.html

**vv. 30–31:**
- Constable: the punishment comes because Jerusalem made political "adultery" with the nations and took up their idols. She receives the same cup of wrath Samaria drank. He quotes Allen, who sees this prophetic image ending in Jesus taking God's judgment on Himself (Mark 14:36). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Henry: Because she has trod in the steps of Samaria's sins, she must expect no other than Samaria's fate. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_023.cfm

**vv. 32–33:**
- Constable notes some call this passage the "cup song." Drinking it makes her an object of scorn. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Henry: the cup is large because it holds a great deal of God's wrath and of the miseries it brings. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-34.html
- Keil: the cup is mocked not so much for its size as because it must be drunk completely empty. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-34.htm

**v. 34:**
- Constable: the same Hebrew verb can mean "gnaw" (NASB, NRSV) or "break" (KJV, NIV, NKJV). Tearing her breasts is probably remorse for how she used them to seduce. Another view is that the broken cup cuts her. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Gill: the shards are sucked so not a drop is lost, meaning the punishment is suffered to the full. He reports and rejects Kimchi's idea that the "breasts" are the oral and written law. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-34.htm
- JFB says she tears her breasts enraged against them as the ministers to thine adultery. Cambridge says the words are missing from the Septuagint (LXX). — same URL
- Clarke reads tearing the breasts as a common sign of extreme grief. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-34.html

**v. 35:**
- Constable: this short message names the root problem, which is that she had forsaken the Lord. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Coke calls forgetting God the source of all their wickedness. He adds that the remnant who came through the exile never went back to idolatry. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tcc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 36:**
- Constable: this closing oracle brings the two sisters back together and judges all Israel. It sums up the section accusing Israel's leaders (chs. 20–23). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Henry: after the northern kingdom fell, many of its survivors settled in Judah and Jerusalem, so the two sisters had in effect become one again. "Wilt thou judge?" means either "Can you excuse them?" or "You are now commissioned to judge them." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-45.html

**v. 37:** Constable: their "adultery" was idolatry, and the "blood" was child sacrifice. They had killed the Lord's own children. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html

**vv. 38–39:**
- Keil: they did not sacrifice children to Moloch inside the temple. Rather, straight after doing it they went into the temple to worship the Lord, which placed Jehovah upon a par with Moloch. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-42.htm
- Constable makes the same point. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Henry on the Sabbaths: they did ordinary work on them, or perhaps used them for sport and amusement. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-42.html

**vv. 40–41:**
- Guzik: the sisters took God's own incense and oil, meant for the temple, and used them at idol festivals. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-23/
- Constable: the "messengers" were invitations to foreign envoys to come and make treaties. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Keil, following Kliefoth, argues this is a new crime and not idolatry. The "men from afar" were Assyrians or Chaldeans, not idols. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-45.htm

**v. 42:** The main question is whether the Hebrew word means "Sabeans" or "drunkards."
- Ellicott: "Sabeans" is not a proper name and should be "drunkards." He reads the line as the invader's noise being quieted by Israel's tribute. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-42.htm
- Pulpit: almost all recent commentators read "drunkards," since the Sabeans were too far away to fit the picture. Drunkenness was a Babylonian vice, and the bracelets and crowns stand for the wealth and prestige the alliance promised. — same URL
- JFB and Poole keep "Sabeans" and see them as rough desert raiders. — same URL
- Constable says both meanings may be intended as a play on words. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Clarke sees an idol festival here. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/rus/rst/ezekiel/23-42.html
- Coffman, citing Beasley-Murray, thinks of Judah's new neighbours (Arabs, Moab, Tyre and others). His conclusion: Judah would have made an alliance with anyone. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-42.html

**v. 43:**
- JFB paraphrases it as asking how lovers could still want so worn-out an old adulteress. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eze/Eze_023.cfm
- Keil: Judah had sunk so deep that she could never stop. The urge to prostitution lives on even after the woman herself is spent. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-45.htm

**v. 44:** Constable: God marvels that the nations still found these worn-out partners attractive, yet they did. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html

**v. 45:** Commentators disagree about who the "righteous men" are.
- **The Babylonians as God's instruments.** JFB says they were not "righteous" in themselves. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eze/Eze_023.cfm
- Keil and Barnes say the same. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-45.htm
- Clarke says the same. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-45.html
- Bible.org's commentary on Ezekiel 23 says "righteous" means "fair" here and does not mean followers of the Lord. — https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-23
- **Other options.** Poole lists faithful Israelites, prophets like Jeremiah, or the Babylonians as "comparatively" righteous. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-45.htm
- Henry adds a fourth: an appeal to everyone with a sense of fairness. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-45.html
- Constable reports that some (Feinberg, Dyer) think it means the leaders of the faithful remnant. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- Cambridge says Ezekiel is continuing the picture of an adulteress on trial and does not have the nations in mind. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-45.htm

**vv. 46–47:**
- Constable: stoning was the Mosaic punishment for adulterers and murderers. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
- JFB, citing Grotius, says the "company" is properly "a council of judges" passing sentence on a criminal. Gill sees an allusion to the Sanhedrin (the Jewish ruling council). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-46.htm
- Cambridge connects the stoning to Leviticus 20:10 and John 8:5. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-45.htm

**v. 48:**
- Pulpit: "all women will be admonished" means idolatry would stop being the sin of Israel's cities. — https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/23-45.htm
- Henry: The judgments of God upon some are designed to teach others. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/23-45.html

**v. 49:**
- Keil asks why the punishment is still future for both sisters when Samaria had already fallen. His answer: the allegory treats the sisters as one, Judah's fall affected the northern remnant still in the land, and the judgment includes later judgments on the whole nation. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-45.htm
- Constable quotes Cooper: unlike most such messages, this one does not aim at repentance and ends on a note of finality. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html

## 2. Differences between Protestant traditions

I found no doctrinal split between denominations on this passage. The disagreements in the pages I read are about interpretation, and they cut across traditions:
- whether v. 25 is literal or symbolic;
- whether vv. 40–41 describe idolatry or political alliances;
- "Sabeans" or "drunkards" in v. 42;
- who the "righteous men" are in v. 45.

I didn't reach any denominational sites, so I have nothing from a named tradition's own teachers.

## 3. Other views

- **Ancient background (v. 25):** a BibleHub article says Assyrian treaty curses threatened disloyal vassals with mutilation. It suggests Ezekiel turns those curses back on Judah, which had trusted pagan overlords. — https://biblehub.com/q/What_context_is_needed_for_Ezekiel_23_25.htm
- **Textual note (v. 34):** Cambridge says the breast-tearing clause is missing from the Septuagint. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/23-34.htm
- **Catholic/Orthodox, NET Bible, Bible Odyssey, and popular movements (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** I didn't reach these sources, so nothing to report.

**For your editing:** Constable quotes Stuart that this chapter requires extreme care in teaching and preaching. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-23.html
